a row means. Do NOT copy it back here; issue 1095 is what that cost.

c:get_disable_loaned_message.why: reads the `ROS_DISABLE_LOANED_MESSAGES` environment variable. No runtime environment on a device, and loaned messages are a zero-copy path selected at build time here (RFC-0010/0038).

c:get_zero_initialized_node.why: rcl's free-function spelling of the above; ours is `nros_node_get_zero_initialized`, a method-style name on the type. The idiom is kept, the spelling follows our own convention.

c:node_get_domain_id.why: the domain is an input to `nros_support_init` and cannot be read back from a node. On a device the value came from the boot ladder (explicit / hosted env / baked), so which domain actually won is genuinely not obvious to the code that wants to log it. Phase 379 W3.

c:node_get_fully_qualified_name.why: namespace + name as one string. We expose `nros_node_get_name` and `nros_node_get_namespace` separately and never their composition, which is the form that matches what appears on the wire. Phase 379 W3.

c:node_get_graph_guard_condition.why: the guard condition rcl fires when the ROS graph changes. `nros/rmw_vtable.h` carries this exact slot, shaped like `set_wake_callback`, precisely so a backend CAN trigger it -- no backend fills it yet. An earlier verdict here said `nothing would ever trigger it`, which is narrower than the truth: nothing triggers it TODAY. NOT impossible -- unimplemented. `nros/rmw_vtable.h` has carried the whole graph family as optional slots since phase-376 W4 (get_node_names, the four *_by_node forms, get_{topic,service}_names_and_types, get_{publishers,subscriptions}_info_by_topic, count_{publishers,subscribers}, node_get_graph_guard_condition), every one is `None` in the cffi backend, and no runtime wrapper or user entry point exists. Both real backends already run the machinery: the zenoh shim declares AND queries `@ros2_lv` liveliness tokens (`Ros2Liveliness::*_keyexpr`, wildcard GETs in shim/session.rs) -- the same mechanism rmw_zenoh_cpp builds its graph cache from -- and nros-rmw-cyclonedds publishes `ros_discovery_info` so `ros2 node list` can see us. We are VISIBLE in the graph and cannot READ it; only the reading half is missing. Phase 379 W3.

c:node_get_logger_name.why:
rcl derives a logger name from the node so rcutils logging can be filtered per node. `nros_log` takes an explicit logger name at the call site (`nros_log::get_logger("<crate>")`), so there is no derived name to fetch.

phase-428 W5 (2026-09-06) — ledgering a recorded sweep finding. CORRECTION, not a new finding: `c:node_get_logger` used to argue this row should be re-read as a GAP because `nros_log::Logger::name()` on the handle it returns IS the derived name. Measured false — `nros_log::get_logger` is lookup-only, so that handle is `DEFAULT_LOGGER` and its name is the catch-all `"nros"` for every node. The decline stands on the reason written above it; the gap argument is withdrawn. See `c:node_get_logger` for the measurement and its own disposition.

c:node_get_rcl_instance_id.why: identifies which `rcl_init` epoch a node belongs to, so a stale handle from a previous init is detectable. There is one init per image.

c:node_get_rmw_handle.why: hands out the underlying `rmw_node_t` so a caller can bypass rcl. Our RMW seam is the vtable in `nros/rmw_vtable.h` (RFC-0035) and is not reachable through a node handle; reaching past the API is how an image ends up depending on which backend it linked.

c:node_get_serialization_format.why:
MERGED 2026-09-06 during the phase-428 W10 rebase onto main, from two independent rows that both landed -- main's phase-421 W2 classification (48911988a) and this branch's phase-428 Q1 row. JSON keeps the LAST, so one author's reasoning was being discarded silently. Both said `extension`; the prose is combined here and neither is lost.

phase-421 W2 (landed 2026-09-04). Ours-only, and there is no upstream name to align to: neither the recorded rclcpp nor rclc surface contains the string "serialization" at all. It cannot: in ROS 2 the wire format is a property of the RMW implementation the process linked, fixed at build time and not a question a node is asked. Here it IS a question — RFC-0088 makes the format a provider (`nros_serdes::format`, `SerializationFormatId`), a uORB image and a CDR image are both buildable, and a message whose format disagrees with the linked backend fails to BUILD (`error[E0080]` from the `const {}` check). The accessor is how a program reads back which one it got. Answers from the single image constant today; the runtime path only becomes reachable when a bridge image links two backends (phase-421 W3, recorded as not yet reachable). C spelling: `nros_node_get_serialization_format()` (`nros_generated.h:5372`, cbindgen output).

phase-428 Q1 (2026-09-06) -- `nros_node_get_serialization_format(node)` (`packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:5676`): the serialization format the backend behind THIS node speaks, as its cross-image identity string (`"cdr"`, `"uorb"`), RFC-0088 D4 / phase-421 W2. rcl has `rmw_get_serialization_format()`, asked of the PROCESS; ours is asked of the node because a bridge image (`Executor::open_multi`) links two backends on two sessions and has no single answer -- the case the reserved vtable slot was cut for. Returns NULL when the node is uninitialised or the backend declares no format, and NULL is not a synonym for `"cdr"` (the header says why). A forwarder onto `packages/core/nros-node/src/executor/node.rs:118`, RFC-0019's thin shim. `cpp:Node::serialization_format` is the C++ face.

c:node_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's `rcl_get_zero_initialized_node()` idiom on our type. Counted as an extension for the same reason as `c:support_get_zero_initialized`: rclc, the C reference, ships no equivalent for its own handles.

c:node_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl. `nros_node_t` carries its state inline because there is no allocator to put it behind a pointer; same shape as `nros_support_t` in the init stage.

c:node_init_default.why: rcl's convenience wrapper for `rcl_node_init` with default options. Ours takes no options at all, so `nros_node_init` already IS the default form.

c:node_init_ex.why: `nros_node_init` plus the fields a device actually varies per node -- the RMW selection and the scheduling context (RFC-0047). rcl would express these through `rcl_node_options_t`; ours is `nros_node_options_t`, passed by pointer to THIS entry point (`nros_generated.h:5297`), so the shape is rcl's -- an options struct on a second constructor. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): the row used to say "with no options struct", which its own signature refutes. What differs from rcl is the options LIFECYCLE, not the type: ours is plain inline storage with no pointer fields, returned BY VALUE from `nros_node_get_default_options()` and owned by the caller, so there is no `copy`/`fini` pair.

c:node_init_with_options.why: rcl's second node constructor. The CAPABILITY is present under another name: `nros_node_init_ex(node, support, name, const struct nros_node_options_t *)` (`nros_generated.h:5297`) is exactly this function -- see `c:node_init_ex`. Note node is the odd one out in our own C surface, where the other four entities do spell it `*_init_with_options` (`nros_publisher_init_with_options`, `nros_subscription_init_with_options`, `nros_service_init_with_options`, `nros_client_init_with_options`). CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this row said "there is no options struct to pass", which is false -- `nros_node_options_t` ships and correlates `same`. The verdict is left at `declined` pending a decision on whether `nros_node_init_ex` should move to the family spelling; on the evidence it looks like a `rename`.

c:node_is_valid.why:
rcl reports whether a node handle is usable. We have `nros_node_state_t` (uninitialised/initialised/finalised) and no predicate that reads it -- `nros_support_is_valid` exists for the support object and the node has no counterpart. Nothing prevents one. Phase 379 W3.

phase-428 W5 (2026-09-06) — ledgering a recorded sweep finding. RANKED-23, and it sharpens this row from "nothing prevents one" to "one exists and answers the wrong question".

UPSTREAM'S CONTRACT: `rcl_node_is_valid` is false once the node's context is invalid — that is exactly what separates it from `rcl_node_is_valid_except_context`, which we already decline as a row of its own.

OURS (`packages/api/nros-c/src/node.rs:760`) tests two things: the node's own state, and — only when `is_multi_session()` — the executor slot generation. It NEVER reads `node.support`. A node built by `rclc_node_init_default` leaves `node_id == 0`, so it is not multi-session and only the first test applies; `rclc_support_fini` (`packages/api/nros-c/src/support.rs:331`) drops the inline session, zeroes `_opaque` and marks the SUPPORT shut down while touching no node. So the node reads INITIALIZED, and `rcl_node_is_valid` returns TRUE over a dropped session. The function's own doc comment ("Two questions, both answered, because either one alone is a lie") enumerates two questions where there are three.

HOW A USER FINDS OUT: SILENTLY WRONG, then use-after-free — the guard passes and the next publish or take dereferences the zeroed `_opaque`. `nros_support_is_valid` (`packages/api/nros-c/src/support.rs:362`) is the predicate that DOES know, so the disposition is ADOPT: consult it. Re-verified by hand against the current worktree before this row was written.

c:node_is_valid_except_context.why: rcl's variant for checking a node whose context has already been finalised -- a teardown-ordering hazard that exists because rcl's node points at a separately-owned context. Our node reaches its support object through the handle it was created with, so the split state is not reachable.

c:node_options_*.why: `rcl_node_options_t` is built, COPIED and FINALISED before `rcl_node_init` consumes it; that lifecycle is what collapses here. Ours (`nros_node_options_t`, `nros_generated.h:1972-2011`) is plain inline storage with no pointer fields, so it is stack-allocatable and memcpy-able and there is nothing to copy or free -- the same collapse `c:init_options_*` records one stage over. CORRECTED 2026-09-04 (phase-417): this row said domain, arguments and the rosout toggle are build-time decisions and that there is no options object at all. `nros_node_options_t` ships, correlates `same`, and carries a RUNTIME `domain_id_override` alongside per-node `rmw_name`, `locator`, `namespace_` and `sched_context_id`. What rcl has and we do not is the copy/fini lifecycle, not the type.

c:node_resolve_name.why: expands a relative topic name against the node's namespace and remap rules. Ours are resolved at codegen/launch time (RFC-0046), so a C caller passing a runtime-built name has no way to ask what it will become. Real for anyone constructing topic names dynamically. Phase 379 W3.

c:node_state_t.why: an explicit node lifecycle (uninitialised / initialised / finalised) so double-init and use-after-fini return a code instead of being undefined. See `c:support_state_t`.

c:node_visit_fn.why: phase-381 W4. The ours-half of the `names_and_types_t` / `topic_endpoint_info_array_t` divergence already recorded in this file: upstream returns `rcutils_string_array_t` / `rmw_names_and_types_t`, which allocate two levels deep. There is no allocator at this seam, and a caller-provided buffer needs a bound the CALLER cannot know -- the graph has no such bound. So enumeration is a VISITOR: peak extra memory is one entry, the backend streams from state it already holds, every string is borrowed for the call, and a caller with its own limit stops early by returning false.

cpp:ComponentNode.why: RFC-0044's IS-A-node authoring base: a user writes `class Talker : public nros::ComponentNode` and wires its entities in the ctor body, which is exactly what `class Talker : public rclcpp::Node` is. It reports ours-only because rclcpp needs ONE node type and we ship two. `nros::Node` is the value HANDLE -- caller-owned storage, move-only, carrying an FFI handle, with RFC-0022's rule that two live handles are a borrow error -- so deriving from it would put its move/dtor surface on every user node; RFC-0044 Q1 decided WRAP rather than derive, and `ComponentNode` owns an `nros::Node node_` member the convenience methods forward to. Two constraints hold the split in place: no allocator (there is no `std::make_shared<Talker>` -- the generated entry placement-news the component into an arena slot) and no exceptions (a ctor cannot throw on a failed entity creation, so RFC-0044 Q2 records an `ok()` flag instead -- see `cpp:ComponentNode::ok`). Whether the pair should be spelled differently is the open question this row records; the METHODS need no change, and each is filed under its own topic. Note `nros/nros.hpp` does not include `component_node.hpp`, so a ported node reaches this type only through the generated entry or an explicit include -- `cpp:Node::declare_parameter` records what that costs. Phase 379 W5, issue 0818: these rows exist at all only because the extractor now compiles `component_node.hpp` as its own translation unit.

cpp:ComponentNode::ComponentNode.why: `ComponentNode(NodeHandle, const char* name, const char* ns = nullptr)` against rclcpp's `Node(const std::string& name[, const std::string& ns], const NodeOptions&)`. Three differences, each with a constraint. The leading `NodeHandle`: the executor IS the session and owns the static entity arena, so a node is created ON one and cannot exist before it (`cpp:Executor::create_node`, `cpp:Context`, `cpp:NodeHandle`). `const char*` rather than `std::string`: no allocator, and a node name on a device is a literal. No `NodeOptions`: the `compile-time-options` rule. It also cannot throw -- a null handle or a failed `Node::create` sets the `ok()` flag and the generated entry halts boot naming the node (RFC-0044 Q2). See `cpp:Node::Node` for the same divergence on the handle type.

cpp:ComponentNode::error_code.why: the raw error CODE of the first failure, or `0` when `ok()`. The other half of `cpp:ComponentNode::error_what`; see `cpp:ComponentNode::ok`.

cpp:ComponentNode::error_what.why: the failure SITE (`"create_publisher"`, `"node create"`, ...) of the first error, or `nullptr` when `ok()`. Half of what a thrown rclcpp ctor exception would have carried; see `cpp:ComponentNode::ok` for why it is a flag and not a throw.

cpp:ComponentNode::get_name.why: rclcpp's `Node::get_name`: same name, same no-argument shape, same `const char*` return, forwarding to the owned node. It reports ours-only ONLY because the owning TYPE is spelled differently -- `Node::get_name` correlates as `same`, so the method needs no change and `cpp:ComponentNode` carries the open question. Same pattern as `cpp:Client::wait_for_action_server`, where a method we ship reads as unmatched because rclcpp_action can spell its type `Client` and we cannot.

cpp:ComponentNode::get_namespace.why: rclcpp's `Node::get_namespace`, forwarding to the owned node; `Node::get_namespace` correlates as `same`. A type-name artifact, not a new method -- see `cpp:ComponentNode::get_name`.

cpp:ComponentNode::node.why: the accessor for the owned `nros::Node`, and a direct consequence of RFC-0044 Q1's WRAP decision: a base that DERIVED from the node would need no accessor, which is why `rclcpp::Node` -- the thing a user derives -- has none. A component reaches through it for the lower-level `bind_*` / `create_*_raw` seam in `<nros/component.hpp>` and for the entities `ComponentNode`'s convenience members do not cover (services, actions). See `cpp:ComponentNode`.

cpp:ComponentNode::ok.why: RFC-0044 Q2. rclcpp reports a failed entity or parameter creation inside a node ctor by THROWING; we compile without exceptions, so the ctor records a flag and the generated entry / single-node carrier checks `ok()` immediately after construction and halts boot NAMING the failing node -- the multi-node boot diagnostic a thrown ctor would otherwise have given. Do not confuse it with the free `nros::ok()` / `rclcpp::ok()`, which report context liveness, or with `cpp:Executor::ok`. Issue #230 made the flag SMP-safe: the healthy value is the zero-initialised default, so a reader on a core the ctor's stores have not reached still sees `ok()`, and a real failure is published with a release store and read with an acquire load so it cannot be missed either.

cpp:Node::Node.why:
rclcpp constructs a node from `(name[, namespace][, NodeOptions])` and expects `std::make_shared`. Ours has a default constructor and a move constructor, and the node is produced by `Executor::create_node` / `nros::Node::create` into caller-owned storage -- the `out-param-first` and `no-shared-ptr` rules, applied to construction itself. Constraint: no allocator, and RFC-0022's rule that two live node handles are a borrow error rather than a second shared_ptr.

phase-428 W6 (2026-09-06) — disposition, required because this row's SHAPE CORRESPONDS: the name exists on the ported surface and the correlator files it `same`, so nothing in a build says the contract differs. That is the class RFC-0089 exists for.

UPSTREAM'S CONTRACT: `rclcpp::Node(name)`, `(name, options)`, `(name, ns, options)`, held through `std::make_shared`, throwing when the context is not initialised.

OURS: `packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/nros.hpp:504` — `class Node : public std::enable_shared_from_this<Node>` with those three constructors and a `SharedPtr` alias, so `std::make_shared<rclcpp::Node>("talker")` compiles and works. The `nros::Node` construction shape described above is the NATIVE surface and is unchanged; this is the ported one. Two weakenings: the node does not own an executor — it opens on the process-global one `rclcpp::init()` created (issue 0465) and cannot move between executors (RFC-0002) — and RFC-0018 forbids exceptions, so constructing before `init()` yields an object whose `initialized()` is false rather than a throw.

HOW A USER FINDS OUT: the construction itself is mechanical, because the shape is upstream's. The un-initialised case is NOT loud AT THIS CALL: the object exists and the failure surfaces later. Where it surfaces is `cpp:Node::create_publisher` (RANKED-9), whose factories discard the create's `Result` with an explicit `(void)` and hand back a non-null pointer to a dead entity — that row carries the sharper form of this envelope and is where a fix belongs.

cpp:Node::create.why: the static factory that replaces `std::make_shared<Node>(...)`: it writes into caller-owned storage and returns a status. rclcpp needs no equivalent because its constructor can throw and its factory can allocate.

cpp:Node::create_sub_node.why: a lightweight node sharing its parent's context with an extra namespace prefix, used to group entities under one node. It needs a second node object per sub-namespace and an allocator for it; a namespace is set once at declaration here.

cpp:Node::ffi_handle.why: the opaque pointer the C API and the generated entry point pass around. It is the C++/C seam, not something a ported node calls; rclcpp's analogue would be `get_rcl_node_handle`, which we decline (see `c:node_get_rmw_handle`).

cpp:Node::get_effective_namespace.why: see `cpp:Node::create_sub_node` -- with no sub-nodes, the effective namespace IS `get_namespace()`.

cpp:Node::get_node_base_interface.why: rclcpp splits a node into ~10 `node_interfaces::Node*Interface` slices so a component can be handed the part it needs. The split exists to make rclcpp_components and rclcpp_action composable without passing a whole node; our components are declared, not constructed with an injected node (RFC-0044), so there is nothing to inject a slice of.

cpp:Node::get_node_options.why: see `cpp:NodeOptions`. COLLAPSE CHECK 2026-09-04 (phase-417): CORRECTED: this is SHIPPED, not declined. phase-417 W3.f keeps `get_node_options()` on the shim's `rclcpp::Node` deliberately -- handing back the (empty) options object states nothing false -- so it correlates `same` on the PORTED surface. What IS refused is every OPTION on the object it returns; see `cpp:NodeOptions`, which is now REFUSE-LOUD rather than inert. The row survives because `--check` gates the NATIVE bucket, where this is still `theirs-only`: `nros::Node` has no options object.

cpp:Node::is_valid.why: rclcpp has no node validity predicate because a `Node` that exists was constructed successfully or threw. With -fno-exceptions the object exists either way, so it has to be askable.

cpp:Node::make_shared.why: rclcpp's `SharedPtr` factory macro. No allocator; see `no-shared-ptr` in signature_rules.py.

cpp:Node::serialization_format.why:
MERGED 2026-09-06 during the phase-428 W10 rebase onto main, from two independent rows that both landed -- main's phase-421 W2 classification (48911988a) and this branch's phase-428 Q1 row. JSON keeps the LAST, so one author's reasoning was being discarded silently. Both said `extension`; the prose is combined here and neither is lost.

phase-421 W2 (landed 2026-09-04). Ours-only, and there is no upstream name to align to: neither the recorded rclcpp nor rclc surface contains the string "serialization" at all. It cannot: in ROS 2 the wire format is a property of the RMW implementation the process linked, fixed at build time and not a question a node is asked. Here it IS a question — RFC-0088 makes the format a provider (`nros_serdes::format`, `SerializationFormatId`), a uORB image and a CDR image are both buildable, and a message whose format disagrees with the linked backend fails to BUILD (`error[E0080]` from the `const {}` check). The accessor is how a program reads back which one it got. Answers from the single image constant today; the runtime path only becomes reachable when a bridge image links two backends (phase-421 W3, recorded as not yet reachable). C++ spelling: `Node::serialization_format()` (`nros-cpp/include/nros/node.hpp:245`), forwarding to the C entry point.

phase-428 Q1 (2026-09-06) -- `nros::Node::serialization_format() const -> const char*` (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/node.hpp:248`), the C++ face of `c:node_get_serialization_format`: the wire format of the backend behind this node, per node rather than per process, because a bridge image has two. `const char*` rather than `std::string_view` so the header compiles against Zephyr's minimal libcpp; `nullptr` on an uninitialised node or a backend that declares no format, and `nullptr` does not mean `"cdr"`. rclcpp has no per-node counterpart; the process-wide `rmw_get_serialization_format()` is the nearest upstream name.

cpp:NodeBuilder.why: what replaces `NodeOptions`: a builder that names the four things a device varies -- domain, locator, namespace, RMW selection -- plus the scheduling context (RFC-0047). rclcpp's options object is mutable, copied and passed; a builder consumed at construction needs no storage to outlive the call.

cpp:NodeHandle.why: the ctor argument that stands in for rclcpp's implicit default `Context`: a `void* executor` the generated entry reads from `nros::global_handle()` and hands to every component ctor (`nros::NodeHandle __h(::nros::global_handle());`). rclcpp's `Node` ctor takes no context in the common case -- it picks up the global default -- and the node is attached to an executor afterwards with `add_node`. Ours cannot: the executor IS the session and owns the static entity arena every entity lands in, so a node is created ON one and there is nothing to add later (`cpp:Executor::create_node`, `cpp:Context`). It is a two-word `constexpr` struct with no allocation and no ownership -- see `cpp:NodeHandle::valid` and `cpp:NodeHandle::NodeHandle`.

cpp:NodeHandle::NodeHandle.why: `constexpr NodeHandle()` (null) and `explicit constexpr NodeHandle(void*)`. No allocation, no ownership; rclcpp has no counterpart because it has no such argument. See `cpp:NodeHandle`.

cpp:NodeHandle::valid.why: `executor != nullptr`. `ComponentNode`'s ctor checks it and sets `ok()=false` rather than throwing (`cpp:ComponentNode::ok`); rclcpp's nearest is `Context::is_valid`, which asks a different question of a different object. See `cpp:NodeHandle`.

cpp:NodeOptions.why:
the C++ face of `rcl_node_options_t`; see `c:node_options_*`. `use_intra_process_comms` and `enable_topic_statistics` are runtime toggles for paths that are compile-time here, and `allocator` has nothing to configure. COLLAPSE CHECK 2026-09-04 (phase-417): the shipped shape moved and this row anchors ten inherited member rows, so: the TYPE now exists in `rclcpp_compat.hpp` (the default constructor and `Node(name, options)` are load-bearing for a composable node and claim nothing), and every option SETTER AND GETTER on it is REFUSE-LOUD -- a dependent `static_assert` carrying `NROS_RCLCPP_REFUSE_NODE_OPTIONS`. That is why the family correlates `same`: the names exist by design so the diagnostic can name the constraint and the nano-ros alternative. Before phase-417 W3.f they were ten setters that STORED their argument and returned `*this`, so the idiomatic chain compiled and configured nothing -- one of RFC-0089's two live inversions, and the one a parity instrument cannot see.

phase-428 W6 (2026-09-06) — disposition, required because this row's SHAPE CORRESPONDS: the name exists on the ported surface and the correlator files it `same`, so nothing in a build says the contract differs. That is the class RFC-0089 exists for.

UPSTREAM'S CONTRACT: `rclcpp::NodeOptions` is a chainable builder — `.use_intra_process_comms(true).arguments({...})` — whose stored values the node it is handed READS.

OURS: `packages/api/nros-cpp/include/nros/options.hpp:221` ships the type with a default constructor (load-bearing: `rclcpp::Node(name, options)` takes one) and every setter AND getter as a `template <typename T = void>` whose body is `static_assert(detail::refuse<T>::value, NROS_RCLCPP_REFUSE_NODE_OPTIONS)`. The template parameter exists only to make the assertion DEPENDENT, so it fires on USE rather than on include; callers write the chain exactly as upstream does and deduction picks `T = void`.

HOW A USER FINDS OUT: COMPILE ERROR at the call, carrying the constraint and the nano-ros alternative. This is precisely why the family correlates `same` — the names exist BY DESIGN so the diagnostic can be delivered at the point of failure, which is RFC-0089's refuse-loud verbatim.

The row is in this gate because of what it used to be: before phase-417 W3.f these were ten setters that STORED their argument and returned `*this`, so the idiomatic chain compiled and configured nothing. That is one of RFC-0089's two named live inversions, and it is invisible to every parity instrument — the shape was upstream's throughout.

cpp:create_node.why: the free function that creates a node on the global executor, so a component's `register` does not have to name the executor. rclcpp's equivalent is the `Node` constructor, which we decline.

cpp:create_node_on.why: as `create_node`, but naming the executor explicitly -- required when an image runs several executors, one per RTOS priority tier (RFC-0002). rclcpp's node is not bound to an executor at construction, so it has no counterpart.

cpp:init_with_launch.why: initialises from a resolved launch SystemModel rather than from arguments (RFC-0046: launch is authoritative for node identity). rclcpp reads the same information from argv, which a device does not have.

cpp:init_with_launch_auto.why: as `init_with_launch`, resolving the bringup the entry point was generated for instead of taking it as a parameter.

cpp:init_with_rmw.why: `nros::init` plus a backend selector -- it names the RMW backend the session opens against. rclc/rclcpp have no counterpart because a ROS 2 desktop process selects its middleware with the `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION` environment variable, and an embedded image has no environment to read -- which is precisely how issue 1050 happened: the selector had an env rung and no baked one, so a PX4 module declaring `BACKENDS uorb` could not say so and the registry's first entry won. The hosted env rung (`$NROS_RMW`) still takes precedence, matching `RMW_IMPLEMENTATION`'s authority; this is the rung beneath it. The plain `init` overloads read the same value from the baked `NROS_ENTRY_RMW` compile definition, so this exists for a caller choosing at run time.

cpp:make_node.why: the value-returning spelling of `create_node`, kept for entry points that can take the move.

rust:ActionExecutor.why: machinery `nros::node!` expands into. c:node_init.why:
phase-428 Q1 (2026-09-06) -- `rcl_node_init(node, name, namespace_, context, options)`. No symbol answers to this key: `rcl_node_init` was never exported, and the old `nros_node_init(node, support, name, namespace_)` forwarder was RETIRED at phase-417 stage 6 step B (`packages/api/nros-c/src/node.rs:362-384` records why -- its parameter order was a pure permutation of rclc's, and in C a swapped pointer argument is a WARNING, so the identifier had to go for a stale call to fail at all).

WHAT A PORTING USER WRITES INSTEAD: an rclc file never calls `rcl_node_init` directly; it calls `rclc_node_init_default(node, name, namespace_, support)`, which is `c:node_init_default` (adopt, `packages/api/nros-c/src/node.rs:405`). The options-bearing form is `nros_node_init_ex(node, support, name, options)` (`c:node_init_ex`, `packages/api/nros-c/include/nros/nros_generated.h:5601`). The `context` argument has no counterpart because `nros_support_t` IS the context (`c:support_*`), and the options LIFECYCLE (init/copy/fini) collapses into an inline struct -- `c:node_options_*` has the constraint.

ABSENT rather than adopt-bounded, stated because the obvious label is the other one: adopt-bounded promises the NAME exists with a weaker contract, and `rcl_node_init` does not exist here. A ported call gets `implicit declaration` and the rclc spelling one line away.
